Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from a novel about starting a new school.

Mei stood at the classroom door clutching a timetable she had folded so many times it was soft as cloth.
Twenty-eight faces turned. Someone laughed – not at her, probably, but her cheeks burned anyway.
"There's a seat here," said a girl with silver braces and paint on her fingers. She shoved a pile of comics aside. "I'm Zara. Do you like drawing? Please say yes. Nobody here likes drawing."
Mei, who had filled three sketchbooks on the plane from Shanghai, almost smiled.
"Yes," she said. It was the first word she had spoken all day.

How does the writer present Mei's feelings on her first day at a new school?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: Point: Mei is presented as anxious and isolated. Evidence: the timetable folded until "soft as cloth" and her "cheeks burned anyway". Explanation: the simile reveals repeated nervous handling and the physical blush shows embarrassment even when she is not sure she is being mocked ("probably"). The short sentence "Twenty-eight faces turned" emphasises sudden attention. Zara's chatter about drawing creates hope, and the final line reveals that "Yes" is her first word all day, a turning point towards belonging.

Explanation: the simile reveals repeated nervous handling and the physical blush shows embarrassment even when she is not sure she is being mocked ("probably"). The short sentence "Twenty-eight faces turned" emphasises sudden attention. Zara's chatter about drawing creates hope, and the final line reveals that "Yes" is her first word all day, a turning point towards belonging. Criterion A (scaled to 5): 5 perceptive analysis of several choices with precise evidence; 3-4 substantial; 2 adequate; 1 limited.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: storyboard description of a 30-second charity video advertisement.

SHOT 1 (close-up): A girl's feet in torn sandals walk along a dry riverbed. Sound: wind, no music.
SHOT 2 (wide shot): She carries a yellow jerrycan towards a distant well. Caption: "Amina walks 6 km for water. Every day."
SHOT 3 (close-up): Water pours from a new tap; Amina laughs. Music begins – soft piano.
SHOT 4: Text on screen: "£25 can bring clean water to a child for life."
VOICE-OVER: "Amina's walk can end today." Logo and website.

How does the video advertisement use camera shots, sound and words to persuade viewers to donate?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: Close-ups of torn sandals build empathy, and the wide shot shows the 6 km distance; the caption "Every day." stresses the endless hardship. The shift from wind and silence to piano music when the tap appears signals hope, and the close-up of Amina laughing makes the change personal. The voice-over "Amina's walk can end today" and the price give viewers a simple, immediate action.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: campaign poster from a youth environmental group.

[Image: a mountain of discarded clothes in a desert; a single price tag in the foreground reads "€4.99".]
WORN ONCE. THROWN AWAY. STILL HERE IN 200 YEARS.
The world buys about 80 billion new garments a year.
Before you buy, ask: Do I need it? Will I wear it 30 times?
#ThinkBeforeYouThread  –  Fashion Forward Youth Network

Text B: leaflet from a school eco-club in Singapore.

GO PLASTIC-FREE THIS JULY!
Did you know? Our canteen throws away about 900 plastic cups every week. That's over 30,000 a year – enough to reach the top of Marina Bay Sands if you stacked them!
What can YOU do?
• Bring a reusable bottle (free refills at the new water fountains).
• Say "no straw, please".
• Join our Thursday lunchtime clean-up.
Small changes. Big difference. Sign up at the eco-club table by Friday!

Compare how the two texts persuade young people to change their habits to protect the environment. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both use shocking statistics (80 billion garments; 900 cups a week), short imperatives or questions, and a hashtag or sign-up call to action. Text A is more confrontational: the image of a clothes mountain and the tricolon "WORN ONCE. THROWN AWAY. STILL HERE IN 200 YEARS." create guilt. Text B is more upbeat and local: exclamation marks, a Marina Bay Sands comparison and the reassuring antithesis "Small changes. Big difference." Text A targets global consumer habits; Text B targets a school community with concrete actions.

Text A is more confrontational: the image of a clothes mountain and the tricolon "WORN ONCE. THROWN AWAY. STILL HERE IN 200 YEARS." create guilt. C Producing text: insight, imagination and personal engagement; deliberate stylistic choices; relevant detail and examples. D Using language: varied, accurate vocabulary, sentence structures and forms of expression; appropriate register and style; accurate grammar, spelling and punctuation. 7-8 perceptive/excellent; 5-6 substantial; 3-4 adequate; 1-2 limited. (A 8, B 4, D 8 scaled to 20.)

Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: extract from the autobiography of a cricket coach who grew up in Colombo.

I learned to bat with a coconut-palm branch and a tennis ball wrapped in electrical tape. Our pitch was the lane behind my uncle's shop, and the stumps were a stack of bricks.
The rules were simple: hit the shop window and you were out – and you also had to explain it to my uncle.
I was eleven when I hit the window. I still remember the sound: not a crash, but a tiny, terrible click.
My uncle didn't shout. He handed me a broom and said, 'Now you learn to sweep, then you learn to aim.' I have been coaching young players with that sentence for thirty years.

How does the writer make this childhood memory vivid and meaningful?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: Specific details – the coconut-palm bat, the taped ball, the stack of bricks – recreate the improvised street game. The humorous rule foreshadows the incident, and the unexpected sound "a tiny, terrible click" captures his dread. The uncle's calm words become a lesson, and the final reflection links the anecdote to thirty years of coaching.

The humorous rule foreshadows the incident, and the unexpected sound "a tiny, terrible click" captures his dread. The uncle's calm words become a lesson, and the final reflection links the anecdote to thirty years of coaching. Criterion A (scaled to 5): 5 perceptive analysis of several choices with precise evidence; 3-4 substantial; 2 adequate; 1 limited.

Task 1 – Analysis. Text B: speech by a 14-year-old to a regional youth climate conference in Fiji.

Bula, everyone. My name is Losana, and my island is disappearing.
Not in a hundred years. Now. Last year, the sea came into my grandmother's kitchen. Twice.
Some people say: you are just a child, what can you do? I say: I am a child, and that is exactly why I am here. Because it is my future you are spending.
So I ask you three things: listen to islands, cut emissions, and fund the walls that keep the sea out of kitchens.
Vinaka vakalevu – thank you.

How does Losana make her speech powerful for her audience?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: She opens with a shocking personal hook and short sentences ("Not in a hundred years. Now.") that stress urgency. The concrete image of the sea in her grandmother's kitchen gives emotional evidence. She anticipates the objection "you are just a child" and rebuts it, and finishes with a memorable tricolon of demands, using Fijian greetings to frame the speech with her identity.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: short biography of the environmental activist Wangari Maathai.

Wangari Maathai was born in 1940 in a village in central Kenya, where she fetched water from a stream lined with fig trees.
In 1971 she became the first woman in East and Central Africa to earn a doctorate. But she noticed that the streams of her childhood were drying up as forests were cut down.
In 1977 she founded the Green Belt Movement, paying rural women to plant trees. Together they planted tens of millions.
In 2004 she became the first African woman to win the Nobel Peace Prize.

Text B: short biography of the athlete Jesse Owens.

Jesse Owens was born in Alabama in 1913, the grandson of enslaved people. His family moved north to Ohio, where a school coach noticed how fast he ran.
In 1936 the Olympic Games were held in Berlin. Germany's Nazi government wanted the Games to show that its idea of racial superiority was true.
Owens won four gold medals – in the 100 metres, 200 metres, long jump and relay.
Yet when he returned to the United States, he still faced segregation. 'I wasn't invited to shake hands with the President,' he later said.

Compare how the two biographies present people who overcame challenges. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both are chronological, third-person biographies using dates and achievements. Text A presents Maathai's achievements as a series of "firsts" and links her childhood memories to her environmental work. Text B places Owens's victories in the context of Nazi propaganda and American segregation, using irony ("Yet...") and his own quotation to show injustice. Maathai changed her society; Owens challenged racism abroad but still faced it at home.

Text A presents Maathai's achievements as a series of "firsts" and links her childhood memories to her environmental work. Maathai changed her society; Owens challenged racism abroad but still faced it at home. MYP criteria (each 0-8, scaled to this item). items.stem:
Task 1 – Analysis. Text A: retelling of the Chinese creation myth of Pangu.

In the beginning there was only a great egg, and inside it slept Pangu.
For eighteen thousand years he grew, until one day he stretched and the egg cracked open. The light, clear parts floated up and became the sky; the heavy, dark parts sank and became the earth.
Afraid they would join again, Pangu stood between them, pushing the sky higher each day.
When at last he died, his breath became the wind, his voice the thunder, his eyes the sun and moon, and his blood the rivers.

How does the myth explain the creation of the world?
Refer closely to the text, using short quotations, and explain the effects of the writer's choices.
items.answer: The myth explains creation through the actions and body of one supernatural being. Contrast ("light, clear parts floated up ... heavy, dark parts sank") explains the order of sky and earth; Pangu's effort to push the sky up shows creation as hard work; and the final list ("his breath became the wind...") turns his body into nature, suggesting people and the world are connected.
items.markingKey: Indicative content: The myth explains creation through the actions and body of one supernatural being. Contrast ("light, clear parts floated up ... heavy, dark parts sank") explains the order of sky and earth; Pangu's effort to push the sky up shows creation as hard work; and the final list ("his breath became the wind...") turns his body into nature, suggesting people and the world are connected. Criterion A (scaled to 5): 5 perceptive analysis of several choices with precise evidence; 3-4 substantial; 2 adequate; 1 limited.

Task 1 – Comparative analysis. Text A: travel blog post by a 15-year-old visiting Iceland.

Day 4: I Stood Next to a Volcano (and Lived)
Posted by @nadia_explores
OK, so technically the eruption at Fagradalsfjall had stopped. But the ground was still breathing. Steam curled out of black rock like the earth was exhaling after a long run.
Our guide, Sigga, said the lava field was younger than me. I didn't know rocks could be younger than me!!
My boots smelled of sulphur (rotten eggs, basically) for two days. Worth it.
Drop a 🌋 in the comments if Iceland is on your list!

Text B: diary entry by a 13-year-old on a school expedition in the Scottish Highlands.

Wednesday 14 May
Today was the WORST and maybe the BEST day of my life.
We walked 18 km in the rain. My boots filled with water like two buckets. Leo's map blew into a loch. We argued for twenty minutes about which way was north.
Then the clouds split open and there it was: the whole valley, gold and green, with a rainbow sitting on it like a crown.
Nobody said anything for ages. Even Leo stopped complaining.
Tomorrow: 22 km. Help.

Compare how the two writers present an encounter with the natural world. Write a comparative response that analyses both texts, using evidence and comparative connectives.
items.answer: Both are first-person, informal, humorous accounts of a challenging outdoor experience. Text A (blog) addresses a public audience with emoji, a handle and a comment invitation, and uses personification ("the ground was still breathing") to make the volcano alive. Text B (private diary) moves from comic misery ("like two buckets") to awe at the valley ("a rainbow ... like a crown"). Difference: the blog performs for followers; the diary records honest private feelings, including a moment of silent wonder.

Mark mainly against criterion C (Producing text) and D (Using language), with B (Organising). 7-8 equivalent: imaginative, insightful response with deliberate stylistic choices for effect, a controlled structure and varied, precise, accurate language; 5-6: substantial engagement and mostly effective choices; 3-4: adequate but uneven; 1-2: limited, with frequent errors that obscure meaning.
